metadata.note: deep-explainer, 4-act documentary entirely sourced from ai1-cli/chapters/01-inventory-research-blueprint-signoff.md (read in full) — a single chapter chosen deliberately over spanning multiple chapters, because it is itself a 4-part framework (inventory / research / blueprint / sign-off), satisfying the genre's own multi-act trigger without new-source research risk. NO MANIM on this machine (pangocairo/pkg-config not installed) — the MANIM lane's ~25-40% share is absorbed into REMOTION per beat, documented in BUILD-LOG.md; VOX quota (6/28 body beats = 21%) is honored for real with 6 real archival photographs (Wikimedia Commons, all public-domain or CC-licensed — see SOURCES.md and each media/<BID>.source.txt). Every quote and number is verbatim or near-verbatim from the source chapter — see FACTCHECK.md. GATE P: PENDING, see PEDAGOGY.md.

beats.act: cold open
beats.narration_text: Habari — this is Liam, in for Bear. One real book-building system claims a book is a few hundred decisions wearing a table of contents — and that before a single new chapter drafts, it runs the plan through four gates. I asked Claude to walk me through all four, in order.

command types itself in: the four-gates question
send arms, runningText plays
RESULT lines land in sequence

props.command: Walk me through the four gates a new book has to clear before a single chapter drafts — in order, with real examples.
output: each one has a real catch to show
the last gate the agent can't do itself

beats.act: Act I — Read Before You Trust
beats.narration_text: Act one: read before you trust — the inventory gate.

show.event: act card settles: 'I — Read Before You Trust'

beats.act: Act I — Read Before You Trust
beats.narration_text: Before anything else, someone has to read the old book — not skim it, not trust its table of contents. Twenty-four chapters, each opened and read, and the reader has to say, honestly, in one line, what it actually teaches.

shot.prompt: real archival reading-room photograph — already sourced, see media/A1-1.source.txt

show.event: treated plate; slow push into the reading room
serif label lands: 'read it, don't trust the title'

beats.act: Act I — Read Before You Trust
beats.narration_text: Here's where that discipline earned its keep. The first pass on chapter seventeen read: 'a longer, more in-depth version of the profile.' Read the actual chapter, though, and it's a qualitative-research chapter — methods, ethics — not a bigger profile. One wrong row, caught by actually reading.

show.event: two tracks diverge: the first-pass line arcs up warn, the correction arcs down good

tracks.label: First pass
tracks.outcome: 'a longer, more in-depth version of the profile'
notes: a title restatement wearing a disguise

beats.act: Act I — Read Before You Trust
beats.narration_text: The scale of it: twenty-four chapters, roughly one hundred seventeen thousand words, a median of about five thousand words per chapter. That's the whole shelf someone has to actually read before the new book gets to exist.

shot.prompt: real archival library-stacks photograph — already sourced, see media/A1-3.source.txt

show.event: treated plate; slow drift down the stacks
serif label lands: '24 chapters, ~117,000 words'

beats.act: Act I — Read Before You Trust
beats.narration_text: Three real rows from the actual table: interview portraits, fact-based reports, and the corrected row — because the chapter's own rule holds here too: the inventory is a claim, and you just checked it.

show.event: three chips snap in, one per real inventory row

items: Ch07 — Profile: interview portrait, one controlling sentence
Ch10 — Analytical Report: writing from facts alone
Ch17 — corrected: qualitative research, not a bigger profile
props.caption: the inventory is a claim, and you just checked it

beats.act: Act I — Read Before You Trust
beats.narration_text: Even the person running this left a note in the margin — an honest first pass, not pretending to be final. The margin, the chapter says, is part of the record too, not decoration.

show.event: the quote settles as a single card

items: "It's long. I like it — I'll almost certainly cut it down later. I don't really know what I want to cut until it's written."
props.caption: the author's own margin note, kept in the record

beats.act: Act I — Read Before You Trust
beats.narration_text: One rule closes the gate: the inventory's job is to be true, not to be the plan. What happens with that truth is the next gate's problem entirely.

show.event: the closing line settles

items: the inventory's job is to be true, not to be the plan
props.caption: gate one, closed — on to research

beats.act: Act II — Believe Nothing Once
beats.narration_text: Act two: believe nothing once — the research gate.

show.event: act card settles: 'II — Believe Nothing Once'

beats.act: Act II — Believe Nothing Once
beats.narration_text: Research here isn't one fluent answer trusted on sight. The same plain question runs through three independent systems — and the person asking is the only one with access to all three, so triangulation isn't a luxury, it's the method.

shot.prompt: real archival surveying/triangulation-instrument photograph — already sourced, see media/A2-1.source.txt

show.event: treated plate; slow push into the instrument
serif label lands: 'triangulate, don't trust one answer'

beats.act: Act II — Believe Nothing Once
beats.narration_text: The first research prompt was genuinely impressive — nested categories, a graded rubric, tiered sourcing. And the author's honest verdict killed it in one sentence: 'I don't understand that prompt at all.'

show.event: question settles, two branches draw on
outcome cards land, resolver bar lands last

data.question: An elaborate prompt, or a plain one?

branches.label: The plain replacement
branches.detail: four questions a stranger could answer

resolver.label: Rejected on the spot
resolver.detail: "I don't understand that prompt at all."

beats.act: Act II — Believe Nothing Once
beats.narration_text: A prompt the human can't read is a prompt the human can't judge. So it got rewritten — four plain questions, in language a stranger could answer, this time in about two minutes.

shot.prompt: real archival writing-desk photograph — already sourced, see media/A2-3.source.txt

show.event: treated plate; slow push into the desk
serif label lands: 'a prompt you can't read, you can't judge'

beats.act: Act II — Believe Nothing Once
beats.narration_text: Three marks sort every claim that came back: two independent agreements, a flat disagreement, and an unverifiable specific — fenced out rather than quietly believed.

show.event: three chips snap in, one per mark

items: ✓✓ — both systems agree, independently
⚡ — the systems disagree
⚠ — unverifiable: kept out of the manuscript
props.caption: one reconciled file, every claim marked

beats.act: Act II — Believe Nothing Once
beats.narration_text: One research run rated every single chapter highly relevant. Twenty-four for twenty-four should make you suspicious — and only a second, independent run sitting beside it made that flattery visible at all.

show.event: the quote settles

items: a grading curve with no failures is itself a finding
props.caption: one system rated all 24 chapters "highly relevant"

beats.act: Act II — Believe Nothing Once
beats.narration_text: The three most contested chapters weren't a research failure — they were the research handing back an actual decision the humans still had to make. Disagreement, done right, is the most valuable output there is.

show.event: the closing line settles

items: the disagreements are the decision
props.caption: gate two, closed — on to blueprint

beats.act: Act III — A Few Hundred Decisions
beats.narration_text: Act three: a few hundred decisions — the blueprint gate.

show.event: act card settles: 'III — A Few Hundred Decisions'

beats.act: Act III — A Few Hundred Decisions
beats.narration_text: 'A book is a few hundred decisions wearing a table of contents' — who the reader is, what each chapter builds, what dies, what's missing. Made up front, against evidence, every later edit has something to check against.

shot.prompt: real archival architect/drafting photograph — already sourced, see media/A3-1.source.txt

show.event: treated plate; slow push into the drafting table
serif label lands: 'decisions wearing a table of contents'

beats.act: Act III — A Few Hundred Decisions
beats.narration_text: Blueprint's first move: name the readers, on the record. An employed copywriter as the stated default, a founder, a creator, and a freelancer — a bias that's now a decision, not an accident.

show.event: four chips snap in, one per named reader

items: The employed copywriter — the core's default
The founder
The creator
The freelancer
props.caption: four named readers, not an assumed one

beats.act: Act III — A Few Hundred Decisions
beats.narration_text: Run the disposition on all twenty-four: twenty-one convert or merge, two demote into a module, one splits — and zero, not one, get wholly cut without a logged reason.

show.event: four layers stack in order, one per disposition
the 'zero cut' layer picks up the terracotta accent

layers.sub: convert or merge into the new book

layers.title: 2 chapters
layers.sub: demoted to a module, not cut

layers.title: 0 chapters
layers.sub: wholly cut without a logged reason

props.caption: every one of the 24 source chapters, accounted for

beats.act: Act III — A Few Hundred Decisions
beats.narration_text: The demoted chapters aren't weak evidence being punished — they're relevant to some readers and not others, and the plan says so directly instead of hiding behind a vaguer verdict.

show.event: the quote settles

items: audience-conditional relevance, not thin evidence
props.caption: why the two demotions are reasoned, not punished

beats.act: Act III — A Few Hundred Decisions
beats.narration_text: One chapter rests on research from a single, unverified run. The plan doesn't pretend otherwise — it carries its own hard rule, right there in the proposal, before a word of that chapter gets written.

show.event: the quote settles

items: verify before drafting, or the chapter reframes around what verifies
props.caption: the one chapter built on unverified sources — fenced in its own rule

beats.act: Act III — A Few Hundred Decisions
beats.narration_text: The chapter's own advice to the human reading the plan: watch what gets cut, and notice if you flinch. That flinch is data — not a feeling to override.

show.event: the closing line settles

items: watch what it proposes to cut, and notice whether you flinch — the flinch is information
props.caption: gate three, closed — on to sign-off

beats.act: Act IV — The Signature That Counts
beats.narration_text: Act four: the signature that counts — the sign-off gate.

show.event: act card settles: 'IV — The Signature That Counts'

beats.act: Act IV — The Signature That Counts
beats.narration_text: Every gate before this one, the agent can run alone. This last one, by the system's own constitution, it cannot — someone has to actually read the plan and put a name and a date on it.

shot.prompt: real archival document-signing-ceremony photograph — already sourced, see media/A4-1.source.txt

show.event: treated plate; slow push into the signing
serif label lands: 'the one gate the agent can't run'

beats.act: Act IV — The Signature That Counts
beats.narration_text: Five things the signature actually means — not a vibe, a checklist: every line traces to evidence, the readers are named, the cuts have real reasons, nothing vanished quietly, and nothing unverified snuck in.

show.event: five chips snap in, one per discipline note

items: Every TOC line traces to marked evidence
The readers are named, on the record
Demotions have the right reason, not a vague one
Nothing was cut silently — every chapter has a disposition
Unverified material is fenced, not smuggled in
props.caption: what the signature actually warrants

beats.act: Act IV — The Signature That Counts
beats.narration_text: The actual approval was three words in a chat window. The signature isn't the words — it's the log line the agent writes right after them, the one future chapters get to cite.

show.event: the quote settles

items: "That looks great."
props.caption: the record is everything logged right after these three words

beats.act: Act IV — The Signature That Counts
beats.narration_text: Two legal outcomes, not one. Approve, and the trail is signed. Refuse, with reasons, and the plan gets revised. A refused gate is the system working — a reluctant signature is the one way to actually fail it.

branches.detail: the trail gets signed, logged, citable

branches.label: Refuse

beats.act: Act IV — The Signature That Counts
beats.narration_text: One sentence carries the whole system, repeated from the very first gate to the last. The agent does the work. The human does the one thing it structurally cannot.

show.event: the spine quote settles

items: "The agent prepares; the human signs."
props.caption: the rule that opened gate one closes gate four

beats.act: Act IV — The Signature That Counts
beats.narration_text: And that's the chapter's actual ending — not a finished book, a signed plan for one that doesn't exist yet. Everything after this gate can be checked against a signature that's already on record.

show.event: the closing line settles

items: you now own a signed plan for a book that doesn't build under your name yet
props.caption: all four gates, closed

beats.act: verdict
beats.narration_text: Let's recap with Claude. Inventory: read the actual chapter, not the title — the inventory is a claim, and you just checked it. Research: never trust one fluent answer — triangulate independent systems, and let the disagreements decide. Blueprint: a few hundred decisions wearing a table of contents — named readers, a full disposition, nothing cut silently. And sign-off: the agent prepares, the human signs — a refused gate with reasons beats a reluctant signature, every time.

beats.act: your turn handoff
beats.narration_text: Your turn — here's the prompt, read it with me. 'Before you let me draft anything from a source I already trust, run me through all four gates: inventory what it actually teaches, commission and triangulate real research on it, draft a blueprint naming who this is for, and tell me exactly what you want me to prove before I touch a single new page.' Run it before your next real project. Liam, in for Bear.
